# Foundation models for graft-versus-host disease: plausible, unproven, and first a problem of measurement

*Perspective — draft for discussion. Figure 1 is `figures/Fig01_perspective.pdf`; every number below is generated by `analysis.py` from a public cohort.*

**Summary.** Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) is a chain of predictions on one protocolised clock, the setting in which pretrained health-record models have helped elsewhere. One transplant centre, however, supplies at most a few hundred events, so a GvHD model can only be a borrowed pretrained model with a very small head. A check on the one public longitudinal cohort shows how easily such a head fails and how readily small gains are mimicked by artefacts. The first deliverable is therefore a benchmark that can tell them apart.

**The opportunity.** Every step of allogeneic transplantation — donor, conditioning, prophylaxis, pre-emptive therapy, second-line agent, taper — rests on a prediction from data that arrive on one clock (day 0), at protocolised intervals, with consensus-graded outcomes. EHRSHOT, built at one institution (6,739 patients, 15 tasks), showed the recipe: a released model (141 M parameters, pretrained on 2.57 M patients) kept frozen, a small head, and a few-shot protocol; MOTOR, trained on 55 M records, reports up to 95 % better label efficiency. GvHD prediction remains single-endpoint risk modelling on registry fields — an alternating decision tree on 26,695 recipients, a convolutional network on 18,763, a donor-selection model with AUC 0.70, a registry model for one rare disease at balanced accuracy 0.58 — and we found no few-shot or foundation-model benchmark for it (a non-systematic search).

**The constraint.** A large centre performs about 200 transplants a year: 1,500 patients in a decade, of whom perhaps 16 % develop severe (grade III–IV) acute GvHD. By Riley's criteria a cohort with 70 such events supports about 3 candidate predictors (ten events per parameter gives seven). Learning a representation from one centre's data is therefore out of the question; the only plausible design borrows a pretrained timeline model, freezes it, and fits a head of a handful of parameters. Whether that helps is an empirical question, and it is the one a benchmark must answer.

**What the one public cohort shows.** The aGOAT cohort (one centre in Tianjin; 584 adults, 93 with severe aGvHD; daily blood counts, chemistry, vital signs and fluid loss; sparse flow cytometry and cytokines) allows a direct check (Figure 1). Severe aGvHD starts between day 16 and day 90, the middle half on days 24–39 (panel A). Every block of later patients was predicted from models fitted on earlier patients only, with one tuning grid for every model and patient-level bootstrap intervals.

*Early prognosis is not helped by routine timelines.* From day 7 or day 14, baseline covariates predict severe aGvHD by day 100 with AUROC 0.63 (95 % CI 0.55–0.71); adding daily-timeline summaries changed it by −0.02 to −0.14, depending on landmark and summary. The cohort's authors report AUROC 0.49 for a two-biomarker day-7 plasma score (67 patients).

*The size of the head decides the outcome.* For severe onset in the next 14 days, baseline covariates with time since transplant and known aGvHD reach AUROC 0.64 (0.55–0.71) among patients at risk on the same day. A head that takes the whole recent window (615 inputs) loses 0.10 (−0.19 to −0.02); no single modality adds anything detectable; a 5-dimensional summary learned without labels gains +0.017 (−0.003 to +0.036; panel B), which lies inside the spread of the same arm when the outcome is shuffled (−0.041 to +0.023, 20 shuffles; P = 0.14). In EHRSHOT's few-shot protocol, label-free summaries leave the timeline harmless but not helpful (AUROC 0.65 against 0.65 for the baseline at 64 events), while the whole window stays at 0.57 (panel C).

*A gain of this size cannot be adjudicated at one centre.* A gate fixed in advance (interval lower bound ≥ +0.01) would pass a true gain of +0.017 with probability 11% at this cohort size, 27% at 1,500 patients and 77% across four such centres (panel D); an 80 % chance needs about 6,500 patients. The cohort's authors report a mean AUROC of 0.78 for their own dynamic model (0.58 to 1.00 between validation folds) and 0.94 on a 65-patient holdout; we did not run that model, and our generic heads reach 0.64. Two apparent gains in our first pass vanished under the controls proposed below: a candidate given a wider tuning grid than its baseline gained 0.03, and a pooled AUROC credited any feature that tracks days since transplant (a model that knows only the day scores 0.74 pooled and 0.50 on same-day pairs).

**What follows.** Foundation models for GvHD remain plausible: the problem has the right structure, the pretraining can be borrowed, and a small head is the right size. The evidence that they help is absent, the effects sought are small, and the usual ways of being fooled are all available. A benchmark must fix before any model is run: landmarks at the day a result is *known*; death and relapse as competing events; temporal blocks; same-day pairs; equal tuning budgets for candidate and baseline; a shuffled-outcome null for every claim; heads capped by the number of events; and a gate whose pass probability is known at the cohort's size. Run that way, one institution can make a complete claim about itself, for gains of roughly +0.04 or more by our sample-size calculations; smaller gains, or claims about other centres, need many centres running the same code locally and sharing only summary statistics. We have specified such a benchmark (GvHD-Bench: 40 tasks, frozen label code, a few-shot protocol) in an accompanying notebook.

**A prediction that could fail.** With a released timeline model kept frozen, a head of at most ten parameters fitted on about 1,500 recipients will exceed a tuned registry baseline by at least +0.03 AUROC on at least one pre-specified task (for example, severe aGvHD from the day-7 state), with a paired lower bound of at least +0.01 on a temporal test set. If it does not, that is the result, and it should be published.

**Limitations.** One centre, mostly haploidentical transplants with ATG-based prophylaxis; processed data with short carry-forward of missing values; our summaries are linear or small neural models, not foundation models; the cohort's own dynamic model and biomarker panel were not re-run; the prior-work search was not systematic.

**Figure 1 legend.** Is a foundation model for GvHD plausible? A check on the one public longitudinal cohort (one centre, 584 adults, 93 with severe aGvHD; daily labs, vitals and fluid loss), with every block predicted from earlier patients only. (A) Severe aGvHD starts between day 16 and day 90 (shaded: middle half); blood counts, chemistry, vitals and fluid loss are dense through that window, flow cytometry and cytokines are not. (B) Change in AUROC (same-day pairs; dotted line: the +0.01 margin of the gate) for forecasting severe onset in the next 14 days, against baseline covariates plus time and known aGvHD: a head that takes the whole recent window (615 inputs) loses 0.10; single modalities add nothing detectable; a 5-dimensional label-free summary gains +0.017 (95% CI -0.003 to +0.036), which sits inside the spread of the same arm when the outcome is shuffled (grey bar: central 95% of 20 shuffles; P = 0.14). (C) EHRSHOT-style few-shot curves (mean of three blocks and 25 draws): label-free summaries make the timeline harmless, not helpful; the whole window is harmful. (D) Chance that a gate fixed in advance (interval lower bound at least +0.01) is passed at the observed standard error, by cohort size: the observed gain would pass 11% of the time at this cohort size and 27% at 1,500 patients.
